summary: Specifies the instruction set architecture for BPF, also called eBPF, a technology that began in the Linux kernel and lets untrusted programs run in a privileged context such as an operating system kernel. The name is no longer an acronym for anything.

eli5.summary: Some computers let you add tiny programs inside their brains to do jobs fast. This is the list of the exact simple commands those tiny programs may use.

questions: what is the ebpf instruction set
how big is a bpf instruction
subtitle: The standard instruction set for BPF programs: how each 64-bit instruction is laid out and what it does.

tldr.problem: BPF lets untrusted programs run inside privileged software such as an operating system kernel, but the instruction set that runtimes, compilers and tools rely on had no standard specification.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines fixed 64-bit (or 128-bit wide) instruction encodings, instruction classes, arithmetic, jump, load, store and atomic operations, and named conformance groups, plus two IANA registries for groups and instructions.
tldr.outcome: Implementations must support the base32 group and may add others, so tools can discover what a runtime supports. Verifiers, helper functions and maps are left to other documents.

today: RFC 9669 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC, so it is the current specification of the BPF instruction set. The RFC says that documenting verifier expectations and standardizing helper functions and BTF are left to future work.

sections.title: What BPF Is
sections.content:
eBPF, also commonly called BPF, is a technology with origins in the Linux kernel that can run untrusted programs in a privileged context such as an operating system kernel. This document specifies the BPF instruction set architecture (ISA).

The name once stood for Berkeley Packet Filter, but BPF can now do much more than packet filtering, so it is considered a standalone term that does not stand for anything. The original BPF is sometimes called cBPF (classic BPF) to distinguish it from the now widely deployed eBPF (extended BPF).
sections.eli5: BPF lets small programs run safely inside a computer's core. This document says exactly which commands they can use.

sections.title: Notation and Conformance Groups
sections.content:
The RFC writes integer types as a signedness letter and a width: u32 is a 32-bit unsigned number and s16 a 16-bit signed one. Widths run from 8 to 128 bits. It also defines byte swap helper functions such as be16, le32 and bswap64, and sign extension: copy the X bits of a number into the lower bits of a Y-bit number and fill the rest with the most significant bit of the original.

An implementation does not have to support every instruction. Instead it MUST support the base32 conformance group and MAY support more groups, but if it supports a group it MUST support all instructions in it. Groups let tools such as compilers and runtimes discover what the other side can do.

  • base32: all instructions unless noted otherwise; base64 adds those marked as base64.
  • atomic32 and atomic64: 32-bit atomics, and 64-bit atomics on top.
  • divmul32 and divmul64: division, multiplication and modulo at 32 and 64 bits.
  • packet: deprecated packet access instructions.
sections.eli5: Not every computer has to know every command. Commands are bundled into named packs, and a computer says which packs it knows. Everyone must know the basic pack.

sections.title: Instruction Encoding
sections.content:
BPF has two encodings. The basic instruction uses 64 bits, made of opcode (8 bits), regs (8 bits), offset (16 bits) and imm (32 bits). The wide instruction appends a second 64 bits, for 128 bits in total. The second half is a pseudo instruction with opcode, dst_reg, src_reg and offset all zero, holding a reserved field and next_imm.

The regs byte holds the source and destination register numbers (0 to 10). Their order depends on the host: src_reg|dst_reg on a little-endian host and dst_reg|src_reg on a big-endian host. Multi-byte fields (offset and imm) use the host's byte order. Unused fields SHALL be cleared to zero.

The three least significant bits of the opcode give the instruction class: the load and store classes LD, LDX, ST and STX, the arithmetic classes ALU and ALU64, and the jump classes JMP and JMP32.
sections.eli5: Every command is written in a box of fixed size with slots: what to do, which two storage spots to use, a small distance and a number. Bigger commands use two boxes.

sections.title: Arithmetic and Jump Instructions
sections.content:
For ALU, ALU64, JMP and JMP32 the opcode splits into a 4-bit code, a 1-bit source flag s and the class. Source K (0) uses the 32-bit imm as operand and X (1) uses the src_reg register. ALU works on 32-bit operands and ALU64 on 64-bit operands for otherwise identical operations.

Operations include ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, SDIV, OR, AND, LSH, RSH, NEG, MOD, SMOD, XOR, MOV, MOVSX, ARSH and END (byte swap). Underflow and overflow are allowed, so values wrap. Division by zero sets the destination to zero; modulo by zero leaves the destination unchanged for ALU64, and zeroes its upper 32 bits for ALU. Signed modulo MUST use truncated division, as in C and Go. Shifts mask the shift amount with 0x3F (63) for 64-bit and 0x1F (31) for 32-bit operations.

Jumps include JA, JEQ, JGT, JGE, JSET, JNE and signed and unsigned comparisons, plus CALL and EXIT. The jump offset counts 64-bit instructions relative to the instruction after the jump. JMP uses a 16-bit offset and JMP32 permits a 32-bit one in imm. CALL can invoke a helper function by static ID or BTF ID, or a program-local function, and EXIT returns. The helper functions and BTF are outside the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: These are the calculator buttons and the 'skip ahead if' rules. Numbers just wrap around if they get too big, and dividing by zero gives zero instead of crashing.

sections.title: Load, Store and Atomic Instructions
sections.content:
Load and store opcodes split into a mode, a size sz and the class. Sizes are W (word, 4 bytes), H (half word, 2 bytes), B (byte) and DW (double word, 8 bytes). Modes are IMM, ABS, IND, MEM, MEMSX and ATOMIC. MEM does regular loads and stores between a register and memory at dst + offset or src + offset, and MEMSX does loads that sign-extend.

Atomic operations cannot be interrupted or corrupted by other access to the same memory. They are encoded as store instructions with the ATOMIC mode, and only 32-bit (atomic32) and 64-bit (atomic64) widths exist. The operation is chosen in imm: ADD, OR, AND and XOR, the FETCH modifier (return the old value), XCHG and CMPXCHG.

IMM-mode instructions use the wide encoding and a subtype in src_reg. They can load a 64-bit constant, the address of a map (a shared memory region on some platforms) by file descriptor or index, the address of a platform variable, or a code address. The legacy ABS and IND packet access instructions carried over from classic BPF are deprecated and SHOULD no longer be used.
sections.eli5: These commands move numbers between the program's pockets and the computer's memory. Special 'atomic' ones make sure nobody else can touch the memory halfway through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BPF programs could use instructions to do malicious things with memory, CPU, networking or other resources, much like any other software. Execution environments should only run BPF programs that are trusted and verified, and sandboxing and privilege level separation are key strategies. BPF verifiers ensure that programs terminate within a reasonable time, touch memory only in safe ways, follow platform API contracts and avoid undefined behavior. The details are out of scope, and future IETF work will document verifier expectations.

Running BPF needs an interpreter or a compiler. Interpreters are generally considered a source of insecurity, for example gadgets open to side-channel attacks through speculative execution, whenever they share an address space with confidential data, so a compiler is recommended, and compilers should be audited carefully.
sections.eli5: Running someone else's tiny program is risky, so a strict checker looks it over first, and the program is kept in a safe play area.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The RFC creates two registries in a group called BPF Instructions. The BPF Instruction Conformance Groups registry holds group names with their includes, excludes and status, which is Permanent, Provisional or Historical. The initial entries are atomic32, atomic64, base32, base64, divmul32, divmul64 and packet, the last being Historical. The BPF Instruction Set registry lists each instruction by opcode, src_reg, offset and imm. Appendix A gives its initial values.

Once a group is registered, no instructions can be added to it. A specification should instead register a new group that includes the original and adds instructions. Deprecation works the same way, with a new group that includes the old one and excludes a group holding the deprecated instructions.
sections.eli5: There are two official lists, one of the command packs and one of the commands. To add commands you make a new pack instead of changing an old one.

fields.name: opcode
fields.desc: Operation to perform; its three low bits are the class.

fields.name: regs
fields.desc: src_reg and dst_reg, in an order that depends on host endianness.

fields.name: offset
fields.desc: Signed offset used with pointer arithmetic.
